solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Beatles song for which British don't have time

parts.note: B is the standard abbreviation for British
to lack something is not to have it
'doing bird' is British slang for serving time in prison

explanation.surface: A trivia question asking which Beatles number the British supposedly have no time for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time' here is a prison sentence: BIRD comes from rhyming slang 'bird lime' for time, a convention worth knowing.
explanation.definitionFit: Blackbird is a Paul McCartney track from the 1968 White Album, so it is literally one of the band's recordings.

clue.text: One replacing pair of spectacles, maybe, shoots producer's film

indicators.note: replacing means one thing goes in where another is taken out, a swap of letters

parts.note: bamboo shoots are a familiar vegetable
two round O letters side by side look like a pair of glasses; this is what is taken out
the Roman numeral for one, put in where the glasses were

explanation.surface: A note about an optician's replacement glasses and a film producer's location shoots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoots' looks like filming, but it is the plant; the visual pun OO for spectacles is a common crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Bambi is the 1942 Walt Disney animated feature, so it can be called the work of that famous producer.

clue.text: They move gracefully, as now and then at first, does a runner

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of each of the words just named

parts.note: opening letter
opening letter
opening letter
a couple who elope run off secretly to marry

explanation.surface: Graceful movers compared with a runner who only occasionally moves well at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Now and then' looks like 'occasionally', but it is just two of the three words whose first letters are taken. 'Does a runner' is British slang for fleeing.
explanation.definitionFit: Antelopes are light, swift grazing animals famous for their elegant leaping, so they move gracefully.

clue.text: US city: close to park, a monk collected animals

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: final letter
taken as written
a lama is a Tibetan Buddhist monk
a zoo is a collection of animals

explanation.surface: A scene near a park in an American city, where a monk has gathered some animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' reads as 'near', but it means the end letter. The answer reads K + A + LAMA + ZOO.
explanation.definitionFit: Kalamazoo is a city in southwestern Michigan, well known from the Glenn Miller swing number about it.

clue.text: Stepping up, small girl is embraced by Constantine II, shaking

indicators.note: something embraced is held inside an enclosing pair of arms
shaking jumbles things, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: the emperor's name and numeral are used letter for letter
Fi is a short form of the name Fiona

explanation.surface: An emperor named Constantine II hugging a little girl while trembling.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman numeral II is just two letters I for the fodder. Since everything is shuffled, the girl's position inside barely matters.
explanation.definitionFit: Stepping something up means increasing its strength or degree, which is exactly what an intensification is.

clue.text: American blues show, involving tango, something enjoyed in Irish pub do

parts.note: a demo is a demonstration or showing

indicators.note: to involve is to include, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: craic is the Irish word for lively fun and good company
T is tango in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a do is a social gathering or party

explanation.surface: An American blues concert held amid the fun and tango dancing of an Irish pub event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American blues' looks like music, but blue is the colour of the Democrats on US electoral maps.
explanation.definitionFit: In US politics Democrats are shown in blue and Republicans in red, so the blues are the party's members.

clue.text: Stand to reason with politicians after publicity

parts.note: an ad is an advertisement
the DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: A view that it is logical for politicians to chase publicity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the politicians second. The DUP is a Northern Irish party, not obvious to non-British solvers.
explanation.definitionFit: When an argument adds up it makes sense and is logical, the idiomatic meaning of standing to reason.

clue.text: The equivalent of a mile out?

definitions.text: The equivalent of a mile out?

parts.words: The equivalent of a mile out?
parts.note: surface reading: some distance measured as a mile off
setter's reading: the proverb says a near thing is as good as a mile, and 'out' means wrong

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'a miss is as good as a mile' makes A MISS the equivalent of a mile; read as one word it means awry.
explanation.definitionFit: Something amiss is wrong or out of order, just as a calculation that is out is incorrect.

clue.text: Lay on fresh tongue with fine port

parts.note: to dub a film is to lay a new soundtrack on it in another language
A1 means first-class; the digit 1 is written as the letter I

explanation.surface: Serving a new tongue with a glass of good port, like a dinner course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' looks like meat and 'port' like wine; tongue is a language and port a harbour city.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubai is a major Gulf city and seaport in the United Arab Emirates, home to the huge Jebel Ali harbour.

clue.text: Lift remorseful Tamworth thief might give?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a ride carried on someone's back
second meaning, cryptic: a Tamworth is a breed of pig, so a sorry thief returns the animal

explanation.walkthrough: Split as PIGGY BACK, the answer is what a repentant pig-rustler hands over; Tamworth is a British pig breed named after a Staffordshire town.
explanation.definitionFit: A piggyback is a ride carried on another person's shoulders and back, which is a lift in the sense of a free carry.

clue.text: Sailor from China having time on watch

parts.note: rhyming slang: china plate = mate
lo is an old word for look or behold
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A sailor from China whose time aboard ship is spent on watch duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country but is Cockney rhyming slang for a friend. 'Time on watch' puts T after LO in an across answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Matelot is informal British slang, borrowed from French, for a sailor in the navy.

clue.text: Post-holder's minute trouble attracting particular interest

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for minute
to ail is to trouble or afflict
someone's bag is their thing, as in 'not my bag'

explanation.surface: An office-holder's tiny problem draws attention from a special interest group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post-holder' suggests a job holder, but post means mail; 'minute' looks like tiny but is the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A mailbag is the sack that carries letters, so it literally holds the post.

clue.text: Belief one's got to escape

parts.note: one = I, and the possessive adds S
on the lam is US slang for being on the run

explanation.surface: Someone convinced they must break free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' gives I plus S; LAM as a verb means to flee.
explanation.definitionFit: Islam is the religious faith of Muslims, and a religion is a system of belief.

clue.text: In Newcastle perhaps persist, regularly making demand

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: Newcastle is a city in the North East (NE) of England

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Someone in Newcastle keeps insisting, repeatedly making demands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newcastle perhaps' is a definition by example of a NE CITY, which then holds the even letters of persist.
explanation.definitionFit: A necessity is something needed or required, as when supply cannot meet a demand.

clue.text: Parking shown in tatty A to Z, rather yellow

indicators.note: shown in means placed inside, so one piece sits within another
something tatty is worn and messed about, so these letters are disordered

parts.note: the letters used as written
P is the road-sign symbol for parking

explanation.surface: A battered London street atlas, with parking marked, whose pages have yellowed.
explanation.walkthrough: An A to Z is a British street-map book; here it is just four letters to rearrange around the P.
explanation.definitionFit: Topaz names a brownish or golden yellow colour, after the gemstone, so it describes something somewhat yellow.

clue.text: What to do with laundry from breadbasket drawn off line

parts.note: breadbasket is slang for the stomach
blood drawn off from a patient has been bled
RY is the abbreviation for railway, a rail line

explanation.surface: Taking bread out of a basket and washing off a clothes line, a domestic chore scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawn off line' looks like washing taken off the clothesline, but the line is a railway.
explanation.definitionFit: To tumble-dry clothes is to dry them in a rotating heated machine, a standard step after washing.

clue.text: Anon artist thanks lover

parts.note: anon means soon, in a moment, shortened to 'in a mo'
an RA is a Royal Academician
ta is informal British for thank you

explanation.surface: An anonymous painter thanking their sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anon' looks like anonymous, but it is the old word for shortly.
explanation.definitionFit: An inamorata is a woman with whom someone is in love, an Italian loan for a female sweetheart.

clue.text: Figures English actor had played

indicators.note: something played with is moved about, so the letters take a new order

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
taken as written

explanation.surface: Statistics on the roles a certain English actor has performed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figures' suggests numbers, but it means geometric shapes.
explanation.definitionFit: Octahedra are solid shapes with eight faces, and in geometry such solids are called figures.

clue.text: Equally willing to save face in pointless activity

indicators.note: to save something is to keep it safe inside, so one piece is held within another

parts.note: game means willing, and as is the equal comparison, as in 'as game as'
mug is slang for face

explanation.surface: Someone equally ready to preserve their dignity in a futile exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Save face' wants to be an idiom, but 'face' is a block and 'to save' wraps AS GAME around it. A mug is also a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A mug's game is an idiom for an activity only a fool would bother with, one that is futile.

clue.text: Backing of popular independent initially left huge problem for dictator

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the letters are read in the opposite order

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: opening letter
L is the abbreviation for left
OS stands for outsize
a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: Support from a popular independent candidate first caused the strongman serious trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Huge problem' reads as one phrase, but it splits into two pieces. Everything is strung together, then read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Benito Mussolini ruled Italy as Fascist leader from 1922 to 1943, the archetypal twentieth-century dictator.

clue.text: Gather round far end of water wagon

indicators.note: to go round something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: in sewing, a tuck is a fold gathered in fabric

indicators.note: the far end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: final letter

explanation.surface: People told to gather around the back of the water wagon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water wagon' looks like one item, but 'wagon' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A truck is a large goods vehicle, and in British railway usage an open goods wagon.

clue.text: Marathon winner appearing in racecourse

parts.note: a marathon session is a very long one
champ is short for champion

explanation.surface: The winner of a marathon race turning up at a horse-racing track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marathon' is an adjective here, not the race.
explanation.definitionFit: Longchamp is the famous Paris horse-racing track that hosts the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe.

clue.text: Trailer, one splitting near the bottom

indicators.note: splitting something means driving into it, so pieces sit inside another

parts.note: NR is the abbreviation for near
a trailer advertises a film, so it is an ad
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A trailer, with someone splitting wood close to its base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trailer' suggests a vehicle, but it is a film preview; 'near' is not a position word here but a standard abbreviation that gets split open.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is the lowest point of something, its absolute low, as opposed to the zenith.

clue.text: Pair refusing to fight over a drink

parts.note: a CO is a conscientious objector, so a pair is two of them
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two people who decline to brawl over a drink in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'over' places the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocoa is a hot chocolate beverage made from powdered cacao beans mixed with milk.

clue.text: Good book, first rate on Tube

indicators.note: in an across answer, one thing on another is placed after it, so this sends the earlier-named piece second

parts.note: a hose is a flexible tube
A is the top grade, first-rate

explanation.surface: Recommending a good read for a journey on the London Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good book' suggests a fine novel, but the Good Book is the Bible; 'Tube' looks like the London Underground.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosea is one of the books of the Old Testament, named after a Hebrew prophet, so a book of the Bible.

clue.text: End of concerto out of conductor's range

indicators.note: out of means taken away from, so letters are removed

parts.note: anodes are electrodes, which conduct current

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: final letter, the one removed

explanation.surface: The finale of a concerto is beyond the conductor's musical range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' suggests an orchestra, but it is an electrical conductor; read as plural, it gives ANODES.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andes are the long mountain chain of western South America, and range is the usual word for a mountain chain.

clue.text: Traveller cheated one with short change?

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to do someone is to cheat them
Roman numeral one
loose change is coins

explanation.surface: A tourist swindled by someone handing back too little change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Traveller' looks like a tourist, but in Britain it means a member of an itinerant community.
explanation.definitionFit: Didicoi is a British dialect term, now often considered offensive, for an itinerant person or Gypsy traveller.

clue.text: Send off wine with Valentine, perhaps

parts.note: red is red wine
a valentine is a card, an example of one

explanation.surface: Sending a bottle of wine along with a Valentine card.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send off' looks like posting a gift, but in football it means dismissing a player.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a referee shows a red card to dismiss a player, so to red-card means to expel from the pitch.

clue.text: Herb beverage consumed by player banned

indicators.note: something consumed is swallowed up, so it lies inside the following words

parts.note: inside the letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A herbal drink taken by a sportsman who then got banned for it.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the gap between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Yerba mate is a South American herbal tea made from holly leaves, often called yerba for short.

clue.text: They oppose any works by detective writer

indicators.note: to work something is to rework or manipulate it, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written
Dorothy L Sayers wrote the Lord Peter Wimsey detective novels

explanation.surface: Critics who object to anything a crime novelist publishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works by' looks like a writer's books, but 'works' is the anagram signal for the preceding word.
explanation.definitionFit: Naysayers are people who habitually object or deny, so they oppose whatever is proposed.
